newsitem.title: UK: UK taxes to be cut by 4.0 bln stg, NIESR forecasts.
newsitem.headline: UK taxes to be cut by 4.0 bln stg, NIESR forecasts.

text.p: Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke will cut British taxes by 4.0 billion stg at his November budget, a leading UK think-tank forecast on Wednesday.
But the National Institute for Economic and Social Research (NIESR) said tax increases would be wiser to ensure public sector finances remain on a sustainable footing.

The NIESR report, written by Martin Weale and Garry Young, said tax cuts of about 4.0 billion pounds could represent a one penny reduction in the basic rate of income tax, taking it to 23 percent, as well as over-indexation of personal tax allowances.
It said a fiscal giveaway of that proportion would probably be matched by planned spending cuts, leaving the whole package fiscally neutral.
"Our pre-budget forecast suggests that the budgetary position remains precarious," the report said.
Weale is a member of the UK Treasury's panel of independent economic advisers -- a "wise person".
Clarke will deliver his budget on November 26. His stated long-term objective is to get Britain's public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) down to towards balance.
At last year's budget, Clarke forecast a PSBR of 22.5 billion stg for 1996/97. That was raised to 27.0 billion in July and economists said even that may now be breached.
The NIESR report said tax increases of up to 3.0 billion pounds, together with restrictions on public spending would be more prudent to shore up public finances.
It said the odds on the government's 2.5 percent target for annual underlying inflation being met next year were now less than 50-50.

"We share in the assessment that some policy tightening is required in order that there be a better-than-evens chance of RPIX (retail prices excluding mortgages) being less than 2.5 percent in two years' time," the report said.

But since the chances of the target being missed were only a little worse than evens, it expected Clarke to resist calls for a rise in base rates, now at 5.75 percent, until after elections which must by held by May 1997.
If indirect taxes were cut at the budget and the mark and other European currencies continued to weaken, UK inflation could sneak under its target, the report said.
